\chapter{Review --- A Tense You Build}
\label{ch:review-perfect}
\hlchaptermodality{103}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the two pieces of the perfect and say which carries the person.}

Complete ES-C49-repaso-perfecto: name the two pieces and say why this tense cost less than the present or preterite.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Review — a tense you build}

\label{lesson:ES-C49-repaso-perfecto}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new. Two questions: how many words is this tense, and which of them carries the person?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{Piece one — the person:} \emph{he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han}.

\textbf{Piece two — the meaning:} the participle, which never changes.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{regular} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{-ar} & \textbf{-ado} & \emph{hablado} \\
\emph{-er} / \emph{-ir} & \textbf{-ido} & \emph{comido}, \emph{vivido} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{irregular} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{hacer} & \textbf{hecho} & \emph{decir} $\to$ \textbf{dicho} \\
\emph{ver} & \textbf{visto} & \emph{poner} $\to$ \textbf{puesto} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Six little words times any participle you can form. That is the whole tense.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why this one was cheap}]
Every other tense you have learned made you attach endings to \textbf{every verb}. The present has six endings per family; the preterite has its own set; the imperfect has another.

This one does not work like that. You learn \textbf{six words once}, and then any verb you ever meet joins the tense by forming a single participle. A tense that is \emph{built} rather than \emph{conjugated} costs a fixed amount instead of a per-verb amount.

That is worth recognising as a shape, because Spanish does it again. Once you have \emph{haber} plus a participle, the same two pieces will give you more tenses later by changing only the little word — and each of those will cost you almost nothing, for the same reason this one did.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}he hablado, has comido, ha vivido, hemos hecho, habéis dicho, han visto\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until the little word arrives without thought.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two pieces — name them. (A form of \emph{\textbf{haber}}, plus a \textbf{participle}.) The four irregulars? (\emph{\textbf{Hecho, dicho, visto, puesto}}.) Next: when to reach for this tense instead of the preterite — and the answer depends on where you are standing on the map.
\end{tcolorbox}
